Multi-Scenario Reinforcement Learning for Robust Mission Coordination in Systems of Systems İbrahim Oğuz Çetinkaya Affiliation: Grado Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA Sajad Khodadadian Affiliation: Grado Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA Taylan G. Topcu Affiliation: Grado Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Virginia Tech, Blacksburg, VA Abstract As systems engineering (SE) shifts from monolithic systems to Systems of Systems, Mission Engineering (ME) has emerged as a new line of thinking in SE. Mission environments are uncertain and dynamic, and outcomes depend on how mission assets interact with them, rendering static architectures brittle and calling for flexible yet analytically rigorous ME approaches. We propose an intelligent mission coordination methodology integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for adaptive task allocation. Using a Digital Engineering (DE) infrastructure comprising a digital mission model and agent-based simulation, we formulate mission tactics management as a Markov Decision Process and train an RL coordinator with Proximal Policy Optimization to map mission states to tactical actions from realized outcomes. An aerial firefighting mission with three scenarios demonstrates the approach. First, all trained coordinators significantly outperform random and heuristic baselines. Second, single-scenario coordinators can be brittle: the coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario degrades to random tactics performance in more demanding scenarios, whereas the demanding-scenario coordinator retains most of its advantage when transferred. Third, within the same training budget, a coordinator trained on both scenarios concurrently matches the scenario-specific coordinators in their own scenarios and significantly outperforms every other policy. Sensitivity analyses on ignition location, weather, scenario, and training curricula show that the variability represented during training shapes post-deployment performance. This proof of concept shows DE-enabled mission simulations combined with RL offer a reusable methodology for improving ME practice, which can be extended to fleet design and selection from a mission-first perspective. Keywords: Mission Engineering, System of Systems, Reinforcement Learning, Disaster Management, Artificial Intelligence for Systems Engineering (AI4SE), Robustness 1 Introduction Systems Engineering (SE) has traditionally focused on the realization and lifecycle management of complex engineered systems within a given boundary 1 . However, many modern capabilities are delivered by Systems of Systems (SoS): collections of operationally and managerially independent systems that together achieve what none can achieve alone 2 . Research on SoS architectures has made substantial progress in application areas such as aerospace 3 , 4 , 5 , disaster management 6 , supply chains 7 , 8 , and healthcare 9 , 10 , 11 , among many others 12 , 13 , 14 . Nevertheless, deployed SoS often remain brittle. They are costly to modify once fielded, and their performance is sensitive to operational and contextual changes 15 , 16 . Ensuring that an SoS remains effective therefore requires a perspective anchored in the missions it serves and extending to how its constituent systems are coordinated during operations. To address this need, Mission Engineering (ME) has been proposed as an interdisciplinary “process” that bridges the gap between a mission and the engineering activities that support it; spanning the analysis, design, and integration of operational needs and capabilities toward desired mission outcomes 17 . Within ME, two tightly coupled decision problems arise, reflecting needs identified by Raz et al. 15 : selecting and configuring the assets that form the SoS for a mission, and managing those assets during the mission by adaptively allocating tasks as conditions unfold. Coordinating assets during mission execution is challenging due to unpredictably evolving threats and environmental conditions, nonlinear asset interactions, and a combinatorially growing space of possible task assignments 18 , 19 . These factors often make mission decision problems intractable for exact methods such as optimization, and even when a tractable formulation exists, solving it at every decision point is too slow for operational timelines 20 . Overcoming these limitations requires two complementary capabilities: (i) a realistic environment in which coordination policies can be developed and tested and (ii) a decision method fast enough for operational timelines. Digital Engineering (DE) offers the former. Defined as an approach that aligns data-driven infrastructure, methods, innovation, and workforce to deliver high-payoff solutions in a timely manner 21 , 22 , DE relies on practices such as model-based systems engineering, high-fidelity simulations, and digital twins. These practices could supply rich mission data and the infrastructure to address core ME needs via analytical tools 23 , 24 , and they could serve as a testbed for evaluating ME policies against realistic scenarios before the SoS is deployed. Reinforcement Learning (RL) provides the latter capability. An agent could learn a coordination policy offline by interacting with a mission simulation and, once trained, could map the current mission state to actions without solving the problem at each decision point 25 . Such learning-based coordination is gaining momentum, from hierarchical RL for SoS governance 26 , 27 to RL for defense and space mission planning 28 , 29 . Nonetheless, most of these studies learn in abstract or simplified environments, and those that do use high-fidelity simulations do not frame their problems in ME terms. Hence, coupling RL with high-fidelity mission simulations for ME, so that coordination policies are learned through realistic mission dynamics, remains largely unexplored. This paper addresses this gap by proposing an analytical methodology that integrates high-fidelity digital mission models with RL for intelligent mission coordination. Because a coordinator trained in one mission scenario may not perform well in another, we also examine how the scenarios used for training shape coordination performance. Specifically, we tackle three research questions: RQ1: How can RL methods be synergistically integrated with high-fidelity simulation models to enable intelligent mission coordination given uncertainties, and do the resulting coordinators outperform benchmark approaches? RQ2: How brittle is the performance of intelligent mission coordination agents trained on a single scenario when they face new scenarios within the same mission? RQ3: How does multi-scenario training compare with scenario-specific training in terms of overall performance and robustness across scenarios? These research questions directly address the second ME need Raz pointed out: ability to adaptively allocate tasks and reconfigure the SoS 15 . Throughout, we use brittleness to denote the loss of coordination performance when a coordinator is deployed under conditions it did not encounter during training, and robustness to denote the retention of that performance. Mission resilience in the broader SE sense, the ability of the SoS to absorb, adapt to, and recover from disruptions that occur during a mission, is the longer-term objective of this research agenda; we return to the distinction in Section 5 . Building on our previous studies 30 , 31 , which demonstrated the feasibility of intelligent mission coordination enabled by RL for a single mission with a smaller, homogeneous fleet and a fixed ignition point, this study extends the approach to multiple mission scenarios, a larger heterogeneous fleet, and varying ignition locations. We formulate mission execution as a Markov Decision Process and then apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) - an RL-based algorithm 32 - to train the coordinator. To illustrate the utility of the proposed approach, we use a simulation of a notional aerial firefighting mission developed by the German Aerospace Center (DLR) 33 , in which a set of aerial firefighting assets is deployed to contain a wildfire within a designated region, subject to stochastic threat characteristics and environmental conditions, and their tactics are managed under the assumption of perfect, real-time information. By interacting with the simulation over thousands of episodes, the coordinator learns to map mission states to tactical actions, guided by reward signals that reflect the achievement of mission objectives. We train coordinators under two settings: single-scenario training, in which each coordinator is exposed to one mission scenario, and multi-scenario training, which aims to mitigate the brittleness of coordinators trained in isolation. Our findings are three-fold. First, once trained, the coordinators significantly outperform two baselines: random tactics and a fixed heuristic tactic assignment, in the scenarios they were trained on. Second, single scenario training can be brittle. The coordinator trained on the more forgiving scenario falls to the level of random tactics when transferred to a more demanding one, whereas the coordinator trained on the demanding scenario retains most of its advantage when transferred, even though the fleet, its capabilities, and the available tactics are held constant and only the mission scenario changes. Third, within the same training budget, the multi-scenario coordinator performs on par with each single-scenario coordinator in that coordinator’s own scenario and significantly outperforms all other policies when evaluated across both scenarios. The computational burden is incurred offline during training; once trained, the coordinator assigns tactics from the current mission state without re-optimizing at each decision point. While this paper utilizes an aerial firefighting case study, the proposed analytical approach is mission-agnostic in terms of its structure: the digital model, simulation, Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulation, and training pipeline carry over to other operational settings, although the state, action, and reward definitions must be re-derived for each mission. Ultimately, this study documents how coupling a DE-enabled mission simulation with advanced analytical tools can advance SE and ME practice concurrently. 2 Literature Review This section reviews the three bodies of work on which this research builds: SoS and Mission Engineering, analytical methods for SoS Engineering (SoSE) and ME, and learning-based methodologies for SoSE. 2.1 SoS and Mission Engineering A System of Systems is a collection of systems that retain their operational and managerial independence while coming together to fulfill specific purposes 2 . An SoS is further characterized by evolutionary development, geographical distribution, and significantly more complex emergent behaviors compared to constituent systems acting alone 2 , 34 . Although SoSE is rooted in traditional SE, the tools, methods, and processes of SE exhibit several deficiencies when applied to SoS and cannot simply be transferred 35 . These deficiencies stem from the defining characteristics of SoS: independently managed constituents require federated rather than centralized management, legacy systems constrain the SoS architecture, continuous evolution prevents the architecture from being finalized, and the scale of emergent behaviors has few analogies in traditional SE 35 . Therefore, SoSE shifts from optimizing monolithic systems to orchestrating the interactions of a heterogeneous set of constituent systems to achieve capabilities beyond their individual scopes 36 , 37 , 38 , while accounting for uncertainty 39 , 40 , 13 . However, this orchestration does not end at design time. To realize SoS objectives in changing environments, diverse sets of assets must be selected, configured, and coordinated to serve an evolving set of missions. Although SoSE methods have matured, deployed SoS architectures remain brittle 41 : they are costly to change once implemented, and their performance is susceptible to operational and contextual changes 15 , 16 . Architecting an SoS of heterogeneous constituent systems, whose roles and level of integration may change dynamically with mission conditions, is challenging 42 . Mission Engineering (ME) is an interdisciplinary process that bridges the gap between a mission and the engineering activities that support it, spanning the analysis, design, and integration of operational needs and capabilities toward desired mission outcomes 17 . Although the Department of War (DoW) definition is recent, the concept dates back at least to a 1993 NASA report that described ME as “an end-to-end, multi-mission development methodology that seeks to integrate the development processes between the space, ground, science, and operations segments of a mission” 43 . In both formulations, ME ties engineering activities to the mission environment they serve, which makes it well suited to addressing the brittleness of SoS architectures across application areas. Raz et al. 15 propose a three-stage foundational ME framework for flexibly integrating and adaptively configuring SoS across multiple, evolving missions, addressing the limitations of traditional, static SoS architectures. The framework bridges conceptual modeling and analytical evaluation, providing a mathematical basis for managing the combinatorially explosive design space of dynamic, multi-mission environments. The authors further identify three ME needs: the ability to (1) rigorously and analytically navigate the SoS design space, (2) adaptively allocate tasks and reconfigure the SoS, and (3) identify multiple SoS configurations that can realize the mission. Because deployed SoS architectures are costly to modify, much of the adaptation burden falls on how the constituent systems are coordinated, which raises two difficulties: the tension between efficiency and the preservation of each constituent system’s autonomy 27 , and the brittleness of fixed coordination mechanisms and static strategies when conditions change 44 . Addressing these needs and difficulties calls for analytical methods that extend SoSE and ME from design into operation, enabling the SoS to adapt as missions and conditions evolve. 2.2 SoSE and ME Using Analytical Methods One line of work applies computational tools to SoS architecting. DeLaurentis et al. ( 14 ) synthesized a workbench that maps each of the “archetypal questions” recurring in SoS architecting and evolution to a formal analytical tool. Within this line of work, Uday and Marais 45 define resilience-based system importance measures, which guide the design of more resilient SoS by providing metrics for analytical optimization. Davendralingam and DeLaurentis 46 formulate constituent system selection as a financial portfolio optimization problem solved with robust optimization and, in a notional naval warfare scenario, generate a Pareto-optimal “performance efficiency frontier” that maps SoS performance across levels of accepted developmental risk. Furthermore, Guariniello et al. 47 builds on parametric extensions of functional dependency network analysis to propagate operability and schedule effects through dependency networks. Other relevant work in this area combines approximate dynamic programming with a transfer-contract coordination mechanism to plan multi-stage architecture evolution among conflicting stakeholders 48 , 49 . Similarly, the architecting of Earth-observing satellite programs were formulated as three coupled combinatorial optimization problems composed of instrument selection, instrument-to-spacecraft assignment, and mission scheduling 50 ; computing the non-additive benefit of the SoS with a rule-based expert system rather than linear programming 51 . Taken together, these approaches establish a rigorous analytical basis for design-time SoS decisions, spanning capability–risk trade-offs, dependency-driven fragility, and multi-stakeholder evolution. However, they treat operations statically, leaving the operational coordination of constituent systems unaddressed. A second line of research follows a similar series of SoS questions, from describing an SoS architecture, to selecting its constituents, to analyzing and protecting the network they form. The earliest work in this thread argues that static DoDAF-style architecture products cannot support dynamic analysis and propose generating executable models directly from architectural data through metamodel-level mapping rules 52 . Ge et al., treat constituent selection as a negotiation among stakeholders with divergent preferences 53 . Building on earlier work of 54 , 46 , Li et al. 55 formulate portfolio selection as a multi-objective optimization in which capabilities emerge from network structure. Others cast SoS scheme generation as a path-ranking problem on a task–capability–system supernetwork 56 . Moving to the network those constituents form, Li et al. 57 introduce an operation-loop representation and a spectral robustness measure, and Jiang et al. 58 extend this representation to kill webs (which resemble the mission webs of 15 ) and derive a resilience index from the degradation and recovery of combat effectiveness under attack, concluding that decentralization and functional redundancy improve resilience. Liu et al. 59 use Q-learning to sequence protective investments against continuous disturbances. Collectively, this body of work provides representations and resilience metrics for SoS facing uncertainty ( what to build, what is critical, and how to protect it). However, like the first line, it treats mission operations as fixed inputs rather than as decisions to be made as the mission unfolds; even where RL is used 59 , it sequences protective investments made before an attack rather than coordinating constituent systems during the mission. Beyond these two lines, several standalone studies apply analytical methods to SoS and ME problems. Raz et al. 13 use machine learning to predict performance, robustness, and resilience of a smart-grid SoS to quantify their uncertainty. Covello et al. study network evolution empirically in a game environment, using graph-theoretic analysis rather than learning or optimization 60 . More recently, Huang et al. 61 combine large language models with knowledge graphs through graph retrieval-augmented generation to manage SoS complexity in an urban air mobility case. Most closely related to our work, Dachowicz et al. 18 propose an AI-infused framework that uses a real-time strategy game as a testbed to predict mission outcomes, quantify their uncertainty, and explain the factors driving them, concluding that combining uncertainty quantification with explainable AI closes the mission design loop. 2.3 Learning-Based Methodologies for SoSE Learning-based methods, and RL in particular, offer a complementary route to SoS problems that call for adaptive decisions during operation rather than static, design-time analysis. In RL, an agent learns a policy —a mapping from states to actions— through trial-and-error interaction with its environment rather than explicit modelling, seeking to maximize the cumulative reward it receives over time 25 , 62 . Early RL methods scaled poorly beyond low-dimensional problems because of their memory and computational complexity issues. Deep RL (DRL) overcomes this by approximating policies and value functions with neural networks, extending RL to previously intractable problems 63 , beginning with Deep Q-Networks 64 for high-dimensional discrete control tasks. However, value-based methods are documented to struggle with convergence in stochastic environments compared to policy-gradient methodologies 65 such as Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) 66 , which constrains each update to guarantee monotonic improvement; and PPO 67 , which achieves similar stability with a simpler clipped objective. A recent line of work by Chen, Heydari, and colleagues 26 , 27 , 68 , 44 , 69 , 70 applies hierarchical, multi-agent RL to the governance of complex systems and SoS. The shared premise is that SoS constituents are autonomous, so a central authority cannot dictate their actions, yet system-level outcomes depend on how they operate collectively; governance therefore “steers” the SoS rather than commanding it. The pattern is two-tiered: constituents retain their decision making ability while a manager configures the SoS. The manager learns to allocate resources 26 , to intervene in the network structure linking the constituents 68 , 70 , or to modulate the information each constituent receives 44 . Resource allocation has also been decentralized across subsystem managers drawing on a common pool 27 . In some cases, constituents first learn basic skills that are then frozen, before the manager is trained 26 , 27 . A related approach has been carried to competitive platform markets 71 . This body of work establishes that learning-based managers can steer autonomous constituents toward system-level objectives, which is precisely the relationship between our mission coordinator and the aircraft it coordinates. However, these studies learn in abstract environments (e.g., grid worlds, social dilemmas, random networks), and they do not connect the governance problem to mission outcomes. Closer to the mission setting, although not framed in ME terms, several studies apply RL to mission-related planning objectives such as cooperative task allocation, tactical maneuver optimization, and dynamic threat avoidance 28 , 29 . For instance, Yue et al. use PPO to train cooperative fighter–jammer UAV teams to coordinate their headings, velocities, and jamming sequences in continuous, high-dimensional air defense environments 28 . On the other hand, a modular training and testing framework was integrated with the event-driven SpaceSim platform, propagating high-fidelity orbital dynamics, communications, and remote sensing models across multi-satellite tracking and collision-avoidance scenarios 29 . 2.4 Synthesis and the Research Gap In summary, design-time analytical methods for SoSE and ME are mature but treat operations statically; learning-based governance methods address adaptive coordination of autonomous constituents but in abstract environments; and RL-based mission planners use realistic simulations but neither frame their problems in ME terms nor examine how the scenarios used in training shape performance after deployment. This paper addresses that gap by integrating RL with a high-fidelity digital mission model to train intelligent coordinators, framing the result as an ME capability, and explicitly studying the brittleness of the trained coordinators across mission scenarios. 3 Methodology We propose an intelligent mission coordination approach that enables real-time tactical decision-making by integrating high-fidelity digital mission models with RL. Figure 1 provides an overview of our approach that consists of five stages. The first stage is a digital mission model that includes physics-based representations of the mission’s geographical area, the threat, mission assets, laws of physics, and environmental conditions (e.g., vegetation type and density, wind, temperature) (Section 3.1 ). In the second stage, an agent-based simulation (ABS) built on this model, that links assets, environment, threat, and tactical decisions to simulate missions (Section 3.2 ). The third stage casts the mission coordination problem as an MDP and then builds on it to formulate RL-based intelligent mission coordinators for tactical decision-making (Section 3.3 ). In stage four, the coordinators are trained under two training settings: isolated scenario training and multi-scenario training (Section 3.4 ). Finally we evaluate the agents through two different scenarios: Palisades and Pyrenees. We discuss each of these steps in detail throughout the remainder of this section. Figure 1 : Methodological Overview 3.1 The Firefighting Mission Model We utilize a digital mission model and an accompanying ABS developed by German Aerospace Center (DLR) as a testbed 33 . The model comprises three elements: the geographical area, the firefighting fleet and its supporting infrastructure, and the mission scenarios that instantiate them. 3.1.1 Geographical Area The model abstracts geographical areas by using a grid structure; where each cell is characterized with a set of attributes. Cells are of two types. Non-flammable cells contain no fuel and therefore never ignite; they comprise roads, rocks, water sources, and airports, and are depicted in blue (water) and gray (all others) in Figures 1 and 2 . Because they never ignite, non-flammable cells act as natural firebreaks. Flammable cells comprise urban areas (pink) and vegetation (green). Vegetation cells are further detailed by fuel type (e.g., pines, needles, fallen leaves, grasses, and pasture), so that flammability ranges from urban areas at the low end, through forest litter and pine stands, to grasses and pasture at the high end. These differences shape both fire propagation and mission outcomes: urban areas are harder to ignite than vegetation, but once they burn they incur heavy casualties and economic loss while contributing little to emissions. However, vegetation ignites and spreads fire easily and is the primary driver of emissions while contributing little to casualties and economic loss. At any time, each flammable cell is in one of five burning phases: combustible, early burning, full burning, extinguishing, or burnt. 3.1.2 Firefighting Fleet and Infrastructure The fleet comprises two classes of aircraft, seaplanes and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft (eVTOLs), whose characteristics are summarized in Table 1 . Both classes cruise at comparable speeds (100 m/s for seaplanes and 90 m/s for eVTOLs), so they differ mainly in payload, endurance, take-off & landing distances, and access to water. Each seaplane carries more than three times the payload of an eVTOL and can remain airborne far longer, but scooping requires a long, unobstructed stretch of open water, which limits seaplanes to large water bodies such as the ocean or large lakes. The eVTOLs have smaller payloads and shorter, battery-limited endurance, but because they take off and land vertically they can also reload from small water sources, such as ponds and reservoirs, that are inaccessible to seaplanes. These sources can lie closer to the fire, shortening the eVTOLs’ turnaround between suppression runs. In this study the fleet is fixed at ten aircraft, five seaplanes and five eVTOLs, in every scenario. Airports are the only infrastructure elements in the mission model. They are represented by non-flammable cells and serve as the fleet’s bases: aircraft take off from their assigned airport at deployment, return to an airport whenever their remaining fuel or battery charge requires refueling or recharging, and can also reload suppressant there as an alternative to water sources. The Pyrenees scenario is hypothetical, whereas the Palisades scenario replicates the wildfire of January 7, 2025, a catastrophic event that burned 95 km 2 , caused over 25 billion USD of damage, and resulted in 12 deaths over 31 days 72 . Each scenario covers a 10 × 10 10\times 10 km area whose geography, characterized by proximity to water resources and a heterogeneous mix of urban areas and vegetation of varying density, presents a complex mission environment. It integrates four elements: (i) the geographical area, (ii) the weather, (iii) the wildfire, and (iv) the mission assets; and simulates how they interact as a mission unfolds. The ABS determines when and where the fire ignites and how it propagates across the grid, and in parallel it simulates how each aircraft operates in this environment. Each water release alters how the fire spreads, so the fire and the fleet continuously shape each other, and mission outcomes emerge from the interaction of these elements rather than from any single one. 3.2.1 Fire propagation The wildfire spreads from burning cells to neighboring flammable cells at a pace that depends on the cells’ fuel type, the local terrain, and the current weather, advancing each cell through the five burning phases introduced in Section 3.1 . Because of the variety in fuel, fire fronts spread unevenly, so the difficulty of containing a fire depends on the vegetation around it and on the evolving wind. 3.2.2 Aircraft operations To bound the scope of this study, firefighting is restricted to aerial intervention; no ground firefighting is modeled. Each aircraft is an independent agent with its own position, operational state, and class-specific performance parameters (Table 1 ). At deployment, each aircraft departs its assigned airport fully loaded with suppressant and flies to the target determined by its current tactic, where it releases its payload, extinguishing the burning cells within its drop footprint. It then transits to a water source it can access (or an airport) to reload, flies to its next target, and releases again, repeating this cycle until its remaining fuel or battery charge requires a return to an airport for refueling or recharging, after which it resumes the cycle. Each aircraft engages a fire position determined by the tactic the coordinator assigns to it and by its class-level preferences. Given a point-of-interest (POI) selection tactic (Section 3.3.2 ), each aircraft scores the ongoing fire positions against a set of operational priorities, such as its own proximity to the fire and the fire’s proximity to protected objectives on the map, and engages the highest-scoring one. The priorities are combined through configurable weights that reflect each aircraft class’s operational role. 3.2.3 Mission Outcomes At the end of each episode, four metrics are reported: (i) casualties (lives lost), (ii) cost of burnt area (€), (iii) burnt area (m 2 ), and (iv) emissions from the burnt area (tonnes CO 2 ). These are aggregated into a measure of effectiveness that serves as the coordinator’s reward (Section 3.3.3 ). 3.2.4 The Firefighting Fleet as an SoS Although tactics are assigned centrally, each aircraft selects its own targets: as described in Section 3.2.2 , each asset scores fire positions by combining operational priorities and class-specific weights and engages the highest-scoring one. These weights reflect the operational roles of seaplanes and eVTOLs and persist across scenarios, so the two classes retain distinct preference structures regardless of the coordinator’s decisions. The fleet thus satisfies the two principal criteria that Maier 2 proposed for an SoS: operational and managerial independence. Each aircraft is operationally independent: it selects and suppresses targets without coordinating with other aircraft and would remain fully operable if the SoS were disassembled. The aircraft are also managerially independent, because their target selection follows class-specific preferences that the coordinator neither specifies nor overrides. These preferences reflect the diverse organizations from which constituent systems typically originate; for instance, the seaplanes might be operated by a federal agency such as the US Forest Service, whereas the eVTOLs might be owned by a regional authority such as the State of California. Because the integrated fleet is assembled and centrally managed to fulfill a specific mission purpose, while its components subordinate their normal operational modes to that purpose only during mission execution, it is most accurately classified as a directed SoS in Maier’s taxonomy 2 . The RL-based mission coordinator provides central management at the tactical layer by assigning each aircraft a tactic to coordinate the firefighting mission without revoking the components’ operational or managerial independence: each aircraft still selects its own targets. Since this study aims to provide a proof of concept for the coordinator rather than to solve the fleet-selection problem, we deliberately deploy the same fixed fleet in every scenario and defer fleet planning to future work. 3.3 Markov Decision Process Formulation and RL Implementation We formulate the coordination problem as a MDP, a mathematical framework for modeling sequential decision making under uncertainty 73 , defined by the tuple ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , P , ℛ , γ ) (\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,\mathcal{R},\gamma) . In our implementation, the state captures the condition of the fire, the environment, and each aircraft; the actions are the tactics the coordinator assigns to the aircraft; and the reward is the change in a mission-level measure of effectiveness. Each component is defined below. 3.3.1 The State Space To inform the coordinator about the current mission status, the state comprises 49 environment variables and 2 variables per aircraft at each time step (Table 6 in the Appendix). The variables fall into five groups. The first identifies the mission scenario via a one-hot scenario identifier. The second describes mission progression through time since detection and time to sunset. The third captures the conditions that drive fire behavior: temperature, humidity, and wind speed and direction. The fourth provides a global description of the fire: its ignition point, centroid, and extreme points fix its location and extent; the dominant spread angle and the point at which the spread ray intersects the map boundary characterize its direction of propagation; and the shortest distances from the fire boundary to urban areas, water resources, highly combustible areas, high-slope terrain, and the indirect fire line capture its proximity to protected objectives. The fifth describes the fire at the sector level: the area around the fire center is partitioned into three directional sectors, and for each sector the state reports the severity of the fire front and five urgency scores quantifying the threat the sector poses to each class of protected objective. The final group records the current position of each of the ten aircraft. All variables are scaled to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] for training stability. 3.3.2 The Action Space At each decision step the coordinator specifies a tactic for each aircraft. A tactic is a triplet: • Select POI. Points of interest are the target areas to be protected. This element dictates how the aircraft selects its POI from five alternatives: protect urban areas, protect water resources, protect highly combustible vegetation, protect areas where uphill spread is likely, or intervene indirectly by constructing a suppression line that contains the fire in an ellipse. Each alternative draws on its own subset of measures; for example, “protect urban areas” weighs the fire’s proximity to urban zones against flight distance, whereas “protect water resources” additionally incorporates proximity to water sources. Aircraft executing the indirect alternative bypass this scoring and cooperatively construct the suppression line. • Track POI. This element determines how the aircraft tracks its selected POI, with two alternatives: indirect tracking, in which the aircraft recalculates a new POI once the initially selected point is completely burnt or suppressed, and follow the fire front , which targets the point with the highest spread rate around the original POI. Following the fire front engages the fastest-spreading cells, but some suppressant may be dropped on areas that are not actively burning; it therefore trades payload utilization against target prioritization. • Suppress mode.
